newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU faces mounting farm surpluses - Fischler.
newsitem.headline: EU faces mounting farm surpluses - Fischler.

text.p: The European Union faces growing farm surpluses, especially of cereals and meat, in the next 10 years, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Tuesday.

Cereals intervention stocks were expected to soar to 58 million tonnes -- including 45 million tonnes of wheat -- from just over one million tonnes at present and a previous peak of 33 million in 1993.
Public beef stocks were seen climbing to 1.5 million tonnes, from zero before the outbreak of the mad cow crisis in March 1996.
"It means we have to take action quickly to avoid such a situation," Fischler told a news conference after presenting a long-term market analysis to EU farm ministers.

Under the 1994 GATT agreement, the EU would no longer be able to clear intervention stocks by subsidising exports because such sales were now subject to annual limits, he noted. The analysis assumed all GATT commitments would be fully respected.
Fischler cautioned that the forecasts, which strengthened his case for further reforms, should not be over-dramatised. The projections assumed no change in the EU Common Agricultural Policy.
For milk, pigmeat and poultrymeat, the situation was less dramatic, Fischler said, adding that the EU would continue as a net importer of oilseeds due to planting curbs agreed with the U.S.
The report also looked at agricultural prospects in 10 East European countries seeking EU membership early in the next century.
Recovery from the economic restructuring that followed the collapse of communism at the end of the 1980s was taking longer than expected, especially in the meat sector, Fischler said.

World cereals, beef and dairy market prospects over the next 10 years were also favourable with firm prices facilitating EU efforts to export without the use of subsidies, according to the analysis by the Commission's agricultural directorate.

Fischler said the Commission would issue a detailed report on the beef sector next week, followed by a similar study of the dairy sector in time for an informal meeting of EU farm ministers on May 25-27.
